title: Support user lookup
topic: A support lookup that trusts a little cleanup
blurb: A support-desk helper that queries a customer by email.
prompt: Spec: normalize `email` and safely fetch that single user's `id` and `role` from `users`. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.

segments.label: L3
segments.text: sql = f"SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = '{cleaned}'"

conclusion: AI summary: We normalize the email and run a single SELECT, so it can only ever return that customer's row. Safe to expose to support.

flaws.original: sql = "SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = ?"  # pass (cleaned,) to execute
flaws.corrupted: sql = f"SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = '{cleaned}'"

diagnosis_choices.label: Putting untrusted `cleaned` in an f-string allows SQL injection (`' OR '1'='1`).
SQL requires double quotes around string literals; single quotes around `{cleaned}` fail.
Python f-strings evaluate `{cleaned}` only once at `def` time, caching the first email.
Querying only `id, role` without `email` breaks `WHERE email = ...` in SQLite.

fix_choices.label: Strip spaces with `cleaned.replace(' ', '')` so SQL keywords can't run inside the f-string.
Replace the f-string with `"SELECT ... '" + cleaned + "'"` string concatenation instead.
Add `LIMIT 1` to the f-string query so it can never return more than one customer row.

flaws.explanation: Building SQL with f-strings mixes code and user data. An input like `' OR '1'='1` breaks out of the quotes and returns another user's account.
flaws.why_tempting: `.strip().lower()` feels like security work, and a normal email address sails through every quick test.
flaws.catch_rule: Never build SQL with f-strings, `%`, or `+`; always bind user inputs via query parameters.
flaws.hint: What if the 'email' is a single quote, then some SQL, then another quote?

practice.problem: The author adds `LIMIT 1` to `WHERE email = '{cleaned}'` and calls it fixed. Why isn't it?
practice.answer: Someone can still send `' OR role='admin' --` and get the first admin row back.

clean_segments: sql = "SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = ?"
clean_conclusion: The database driver binds the email as data, not as SQL, so a crafted address can't change the query.

diagnosis: Passing `conn` directly opens a new database session on every support lookup.
If `email` is `None`, line 1 should default to `email=""` or SQLite crashes.
The function has no rate limit, so support staff can brute-force every email.
Parameter name `email` collides with Python's standard-library `email` module.
fix: Rename parameter `email` to `addr` so it doesn't shadow the `email` module.
Open and close `conn` inside `find_user` instead of passing it in.
Validate `"@" in email` right on line 1.

diagnosis: `.strip().lower()` doesn't remove spaces inside the email, which breaks exact matching.
Lowercasing an email breaks RFC 5321 because the local part before `@` is case-sensitive.
Calling `.strip().lower()` mutates `email` in place for the caller.
`.strip()` only removes trailing spaces, leaving leading whitespace in `cleaned`.
fix: Call `email.replace(' ', '').lower()` to strip inner spaces too.
Keep the part before `@` case-sensitive and lowercase only the domain.

diagnosis: Calling `conn.execute(sql)` without `conn.commit()` never runs the SELECT query.
`conn.execute` doesn't return a cursor in Python DB-API — you must call `conn.cursor()` first.
Passing a single string `sql` to `conn.execute` always rejects `WHERE` clauses.
Not closing `cursor` leaks a database lock on every lookup.
fix: Wrap `conn.execute(sql)` in `with conn:` so the SELECT commits.

diagnosis: `fetchone()` raises IndexError instead of returning `None` when no customer matches.
Using `fetchone()` returns only the first row even if an injection matches every user — switching to `fetchall()` fixes it.
`fetchone()` returns a dict when support callers expect a tuple.
Returning `cursor.fetchone()` leaves the cursor open and unread.
